responses.mission_1.search:
BFS path length 13.5 m with 923 expanded nodes. A* path length 13.5 m with 700 expanded nodes. The lengths are equal, and A* looked at 223 fewer cells.

In my bfs(), the frontier is a deque and I always popleft() the oldest cell, so cells are expanded in rings of increasing distance from the start in every direction, including directions that lead away from the goal. BFS only stops when the goal is discovered, so it has to finish almost every ring closer than the goal first.

In my astar(), the frontier is a heap ordered by f = g + ctx.heuristic(cell), where g is the number of moves so far (best_g) and h is the Manhattan distance to the goal. Cells that move away from the goal get a larger f and stay lower in the heap, so many of them are never popped before the goal is. Manhattan distance never overestimates on this 4-connected unit-cost grid, so when the goal is removed from the heap its g is already the cheapest, which is why A* returns the same 13.5 m route as BFS. The heuristic changes the order of examination, not the route length.
responses.mission_1.failure:
On the constrained map, BFS succeeded with 24.5 m, 843 expansions, peak frontier 14. DFS succeeded with 50.0 m, 448 expansions, peak frontier 200. IDDFS stopped with resource_limit after 250,001 expansions and returned no route.

One difference in path length is that dfs() keeps following one branch at a time. In my implementation, it always takes the right first, because I push neighbours in reverse so the first supplied neighbour is on top. A cell is marked as a parent when it is first pushed and never improved, so the route is simply the first branch that reaches the goal, about twice the shortest. It used fewer expansions than BFS because it stopped as soon as that branch hit the goal, but its frontier was larger because every cell on the deep branch leaves its other neighbours waiting on the stack.

In the unreachable case. BFS no_path (9 expansions), DFS no_path (9), IDDFS no_path (231), A* no_path (9). no_path means the search finished: the queue, stack or heap became empty (for IDDFS, a whole pass finished with no depth cutoff), so every reachable cell was tried, and no route exists. resource_limit means the runner stopped an unfinished search when ctx.expand raised its budget exception. It says nothing about whether a path exists.

I used Claude to explain how to fix bugs in all four algorithm implementation drafts. I checked the results with the six checks and the full evaluation table, confirmed BFS and A* match the shortest length, and confirmed the unreachable case returns no_path for all four.
responses.mission_2.prediction: I chose BFS and DFS. I predict BFS will finish sooner on the constrained map. In Mission 1, BFS found the shortest 24.5 m route, while my DFS route was 50.0 m because the stack follows one branch deeply and keeps the first route it finds. Both robots share the same 0.30 m/s speed, so the DFS robot has twice the distance to drive. The DFS route probably contains more turns and zig-zags, where the controller slows down, which means it can take longer.
responses.mission_2.performance:
Constrained map, BFS vs DFS:
- BFS: succeeded, elapsed_s 90.6 s, distance_m 23.9 m (planned 24.5 m), goal error 0.26 m.
- DFS: controller_failed, elapsed_s 146.1 s, distance_m 31.8 m of a 50.0 m planned route, ending 5.88 m from the goal.

The result supported my prediction. BFS reached the goal, and DFS never did. DFS had already driven farther and longer than the whole BFS journey when it stopped.

The DFS route fills the middle room with about six zigzags, because the stack keeps following one branch, and the first branch to reach the goal snakes back and forth. The controller slows for every hairpin turn, so DFS averaged only about 0.22 m/s. My retained checkpoint (sample 1462, t = 148.6 s, x = 1.10, y = -2.31) is where it stopped: speed 0.00 m/s, right at the turn around the bottom of the central wall, where the route hugs the wall. Tracking error there was only 0.02 m, so this was not the robot drifting off the path. So the DFS route quality, its length, and the tight wall-hugging turns caused both the extra time and the failure.
responses.mission_2.choice:
I would choose Nav2 Smac 2D for delivery. It succeeded on both maps: 35.8 s on the open map and 73.3 s on the constrained map, which was the fastest or near-fastest on each.

Compared with my A*.  A* also succeeded on both maps but needed 46.4 s (open) and 90.2 s (constrained), because its 4-connected grid route is a staircase. Nav2 drove 10.1 m vs 13.2 m on the open map and 20.5 m vs 23.9 m on the constrained map. A* tracked its path slightly more closely on the open map (mean tracking error 0.016 m vs 0.042 m), but both are a few centimetres, far below the 0.25 m goal tolerance. On the constrained map, Nav2 kept more estimated wall clearance (0.27 m vs 0.12 m) because it is cost-aware.

Nav2 is deterministic. The advantage that matters most for delivery is reaching the goal reliably in the shortest time while staying away from walls, which Smac created a smoothed, cost-aware route, keeping the robot moving faster when it needs to turn.
responses.mission_3.prediction:
Repulsion only (open map): with influence distance fixed at 1.0 m, I raised repulsion strength from 0.7 (social_1) to 1.3. Both previews stayed "succeeded". The path near the person at (0, -1.7) bent a little farther away and got slightly longer (about 13.6 m to 13.7 m, baseline 13.5 m). The change is small because the bottom wall limits how far the route can move, so the closest pass stays at about 0.75 m body clearance.

Influence distance only (open map): keeping repulsion at 1.3, I raised influence distance from 1.0 m to 1.5 m (social_2). The status stayed "succeeded" and the detour became clearly wider: the path starts bending earlier and is about 14.6 m long, with more of the route near x = 0 kept around 0.8 to 0.9 m from the person instead of 0.75 to 0.8 m.

The same change on the constrained map: social_1 (0.7, 1.0 m) succeeded, but social_2 (1.3, 1.5 m) showed "oscillation". The dashed line stops partway because, in the narrow passage, the wall avoidance and the larger repulsion keep cancelling the attraction to the next waypoint, so the robot kept oscillating instead of moving forward.

I also tried repulsion 2.0 with influence 1.5 m on the open map, and it oscillated there too. So larger repulsion or influence moves the route farther from the person only until there is no room left, then the field gets stuck.
responses.mission_3.comparison:
A*: social_2 (repulsion 1.3, influence 1.5 m) had the largest minimum_person_clearance_m, 0.84 m, with 0.0 s of personal_space_s. Its baseline had 0.76 m and 0.0 s. social_2 did not cost time or distance: 46.5 s and 13.1 m vs 46.7 s and 13.2 m for baseline, even though the refined plan was about 1 m longer (14.6 m vs 13.5 m), because the controller cuts the smoothed corners. Surprisingly, social_1 was worse than baseline: 0.71 m clearance and 1.8 s inside the 0.75 m threshold at up to 0.30 m/s. Its weak repulsion only shifted the path slightly, and the executed route (an AMCL estimate, not ground truth) passed a little closer than planned.

RRT: the baseline had the largest clearance, 1.73 m, with 0.0 s personal_space_s. social_1 (1.71 m) and social_2 (1.73 m) are within a few centimetres of it, which is localization noise. The planned lengths were identical (12.47 m) because RRT's random route already passed more than 1.5 m from the person, outside both influence distances, so the field had nothing to repel. Times were 44.4 s baseline, 43.4 s social_1 and 44.0 s social_2, with distances all about 11.5 to 11.6 m, so there was no real time or distance cost either way.
responses.mission_3.recommendation:
I would keep A* with social_2 (repulsion 1.3, influence 1.5 m) for this scenario. It succeeded with a minimum person clearance of 0.84 m and 0.0 s inside the 0.75 m personal-space threshold, taking 46.5 s and 13.1 m. The A* baseline succeeded in a similar 46.7 s and 13.2 m but passed closer (0.76 m), only just outside the threshold, and the weaker social_1 setting actually entered personal space for 1.8 s (0.71 m). So social_2 gave the most space for no measurable time or distance cost, and A* is deterministic, so the planned route is repeatable. RRT kept even more space (1.73 m), but only because its random route happened to take a different corridor. A different seed could pass much closer, and the field had no effect on it.

The person here never moves, so the field is computed once on a fixed position. A walking person can step into the refined route after it is planned, and the robot would need to replan or slow down and wait, which this fixed-path experiment does not test. The trials also do not measure how comfortable a real person feels, whether they would prefer the robot to pass in front of or behind them, or how they react to its speed.
responses.final.synthesis:
A suitable route for a robot sharing space with people has to be good at three levels. It must be found efficiently; it must be easy for the robot to actually drive, and it must leave people enough room. 

Search efficiency and route quality. BFS and A* both found the shortest routes (13.5 m open, 24.5 m constrained). A* examined fewer cells on the open map (700 vs 923) because its Manhattan heuristic guided the order. DFS was cheap to compute (448 expansions on the constrained map) but returned a 50.0 m route. IDDFS guaranteed short routes in principle but hit the 250,000-expansion limit on both larger maps. That resource_limit is an unfinished search, which means it did not find a route. So efficiency only helps if it doesn’t cost route quality. A* got both, DFS traded quality for speed, and IDDFS gave up efficiency without delivering a route.

Navigation on both maps. Planning time was fairly short, so route quality impacted most of the journey. BFS and A* took about 46 s (open) and 90 s (constrained). The smoothed, cost-aware Nav2 Smac route took 36 s and 73 s. DFS failed on both maps: on the constrained map it stopped after 146 s and 31.8 m, with the controller detecting a collision ahead at a tight turn beside a wall. This shows that fewer expansions do not mean a better journey. A route that was created with fewer expansions can have a lot of sharp turns, which means that the robot has to slow down to follow the path. Compared to routes that have fewer tight turns, but may take more expansions to obtain. The robot doesn't have to slow down as much when following the path and therefore, it can reach the goal a lot faster.

Social trade-offs. The stronger field (repulsion 1.3, influence 1.5 m) raised A*'s closest person clearance from 0.76 m to 0.84 m at no measurable time cost. The weaker setting entered personal space for 1.8 s. The field only helps when the route passes inside its influence distance (RRT already stayed 1.7 m away), and it can oscillate in narrow passages. So the best route for shared space is a good search result, refined for both drivability and personal space, and checked on the robot, because a plan that looks good does not guarantee a good journey.

Estimates vs. ground truth. The planned lengths and the grid are exact for the model, but executed distance, clearance, and goal error come from AMCL estimates and lidar proxies. Each cell was run once, so the success of each route is not guaranteed.
responses.final.course_reflection:
What stood out most was how often the "best" answer changed depending on what I measured. DFS looked efficient in Mission 1 because it expanded fewer cells, but on the robot it failed twice: its long, zig-zagging route forced tight turns next to walls until the controller gave up. Planning took about a millisecond, while driving took over a minute, so the quality of the route mattered far more than the speed of the search. That changed how I think about algorithm efficiency in robotics. The cost that matters is the cost of the whole journey, not just the computation.

Mission 3 made me think about the human side of robotics. A collision-free route is not automatically an acceptable one. A person can be safe and still feel crowded by a robot passing within arm's length. I was surprised that a weak personal-space setting actually made the robot spend more time near the person than doing nothing, and that the stronger setting gave more space without any time cost. It showed me that social behaviour has to be tested, not assumed, and that the numbers (0.75 m, the field strengths) are design choices someone has to explain.
